Nick Bostrom might be a professor of philosophy at the University of Oxford, but he is hardly making a philosophical argument here. In fact I don't know of anyone who holds credentials sufficient enough to make such bold statements about the future of Artificial Intelligence - it is nothing more than speculation, and that doesn't require special training, only a platform [TED].

Where is intelligence? Is intelligence something that is contained inside a brain, or correspondingly inside a computer program? This would seem to be Bostrom's assumption, which makes the creating of intelligence a simple matter of having the right tools and tinkering with things until the job is done. Since there are certain physical and moral barriers to tinkering with organic intelligence, this limits one's ability to increase the intelligence of a living person, but with an artificial intelligence there is the belief that the barriers are much less restrictive, that the limits of an artificial intelligence are simply limits on the physical commodities available to such a thing -- with twice as many resources one could produce twice as much intelligence. An Oxford philosopher would then speculate that such creations might spin out of control, or perhaps lead humanity to a new frontier. Once artificial intelligence has been created, it can be replicated and manufactured much faster than human intelligence, something like the printing of an encyclopedia.

Does it make sense to talk about intelligence in quantified terms? Can one entity be /twice as intelligent/ as another, can one devise a procedure to /double the intelligence/ of some entity? This seems to be central to the concept of a runaway super-intelligence being born out of the current AI project. For ourselves, we have techniques to measure intelligence, but only in comparative and statistical ways. Intelligence is measured as a deviation from an established mean, and the mean itself is calculated by performing a number of anthropological inquiries, by testing the recognition of shape, of color, of pattern, on a population where the perception of shape, of color, of pattern have been recognized and shown to have some degree of individual variation. If we use these same tests on an artificial intelligence, where the idea of a deviation from the mean is no longer relevant (there is no meaningful variation in the population of artificial entities, since their differences can be accounted for in purely physical terms of hardware, power consumption, and so on), then artificial intelligence will by its very nature transcend human intelligence. Once artificial intelligence crosses the threshold of a human measure of intelligence, it can double, and double again.

... if you believe intelligence can be understood in quantified terms, and neatly fits inside the brain.
